title: Abner Changes Sides and Is Murdered
summary: As David's house grows stronger, Abner quarrels with Ish-bosheth over one of Saul's concubines and offers to bring all Israel over to David. David demands the return of his wife Michal, and Abner persuades the elders of Israel. But after a peaceful meeting at Hebron, Joab lures Abner back and kills him to avenge his brother Asahel. David publicly curses Joab, mourns Abner with a lament, and fasts, and the people are convinced the king had no part in the murder.
story: The civil war that began at Gibeon drags on, and the chapter's first line sets the direction: David grows stronger, Saul's house weaker. The real power in the north is not Ish-bosheth but Abner, and when the weak king challenges him, Abner decides to hand the kingdom to David. For a moment it seems the whole nation will come to David peacefully through negotiation and covenant. Then Joab, driven by the blood of Asahel from chapter 2 and perhaps by fear of a rival for his own position, murders Abner at the city gate. The chapter shows David's kingdom advancing and, at the same moment, the violence of his own men staining it. It also introduces, in the list of sons born at Hebron, the names that will fill the tragedies of David's later years: Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah.
historical:
These events fall during David's seven and a half years at Hebron, around 1010 to 1003 BC. The list of six sons, each by a different mother, reflects the marriages of a rising king. Most are to women of Judah and its region, but Maacah is the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee. A marriage to a king's daughter was a diplomatic alliance, and it placed an ally on the northern flank of Ish-bosheth's territory. Absalom, her son, will later flee to his grandfather in Geshur (13:37).

Abner's phrase from Dan to Beersheba (verse 10) became the standard way of naming the whole land of Israel from its northern to its southern limit. Hebron was one of the six cities of refuge set apart in Joshua 20:7 as places where a person who had killed could be protected until judged. Some interpreters note the irony that Joab kills Abner in the gateway of a city of refuge, bypassing the very system meant to prevent private blood vengeance, especially since Asahel had died in battle, not by murder.
cultural:
A king's concubines were part of his household and, in the ancient Near East, a public sign of his authority. To take a dead king's concubine could be read as a claim to his throne. That is why Ish-bosheth's accusation is so serious and why Abner reacts so violently; later Absalom (16:21-22) and Adonijah (1 Kings 2:13-25) make similar moves. Whether Abner actually slept with Rizpah the narrator does not say.

David's demand for Michal is both personal and political. She was his first wife, won at great cost (1 Samuel 18:25-27) and then given by Saul to another man. Taking her back restored his marriage bond with Saul's family and strengthened his claim to Saul's kingdom. The scene of Paltiel following her, weeping, to Bahurim is one of the saddest in the book. Covenant here means a sworn agreement between parties, sealed with a feast, like the meal David holds for Abner. The gateway where Joab kills Abner was the city's public space, where courts sat and business was done; to kill there was to do violence in the place of justice. Mourning practices (torn clothes, sackcloth, walking behind the bier, fasting) were the public language of grief, and David uses them deliberately so that Israel will see where he stands.
literary: The chapter is framed by weakness and strength: it opens with David growing stronger and closes with David saying, “I am weak this day, though anointed as king.” Between these frames it moves in stages: the list of sons, Abner's break with Ish-bosheth, the negotiations, the murder, and the mourning. The narrator repeats three times that David sent Abner away in peace (verses 21, 22, 23) so that no reader can miss David's innocence, and adds a parenthesis (verse 30) spelling out the motive for the killing. David's short lament for Abner asks whether he should die the death of a fool, that is, like a nabal, caught unarmed and unbound by treachery. The final verses shift from Abner to the sons of Zeruiah, whose fierce loyalty David cannot control, a tension that will run to the end of his life (1 Kings 2:5-6).

outline.t: David grows stronger; sons born at Hebron
Abner's covenant offer and the return of Michal
Abner wins over the elders and meets David
David mourns Abner and disowns the killing

doctrines.note: Abner, the man who kept Saul's house alive, becomes the instrument that hands the kingdom to David, and he says so himself: he will do for David what the LORD has sworn to him. God's purpose moves forward even through the pride and grudges of human actors.

Joab's murder of Abner is personal vengeance dressed as loyalty. The chapter shows how sin inside the king's own circle can threaten the justice of the kingdom, and how even a righteous king can be too weak to restrain the violence of those who serve him.
Abner seeks a covenant with David, and the elders will make one too (5:3). Kingship in Israel was meant to rest on covenant, a sworn relationship with obligations on both sides, before the LORD.

words.note: Berit, covenant, a binding agreement sealed by oath and often by a meal. It is the Bible's central word for God's relationships with his people, and here it names a political agreement between Abner and David and between David and the elders. The human covenants of this chapter prepare for the covenant God will make with David himself in chapter 7.

Yasha, to save or deliver, the root of the names Joshua and Jesus. Abner reminds the elders that the LORD said he would save his people Israel from the Philistines through his servant David. Whether this quotes an otherwise unrecorded word or summarizes earlier promises, it frames David's kingship as God's instrument of salvation.

Dam, blood. The chapter turns on bloodguilt: Abner dies on account of the blood of Asahel, and David declares himself and his kingdom forever guiltless of the blood of Abner. In Israel, innocent blood cried out for justice, and a king with such blood on his hands would stand under judgment. David's public mourning is a public disowning of that guilt.

Sar, prince, commander, or official. David calls Abner a great prince fallen in Israel, honoring his enemy's former commander with a title of real respect. The same word is used of military commanders throughout Samuel; David's generosity toward a rival who had fought against him is part of the chapter's portrait of the king.

christ: Abner's reminder that the LORD promised to save his people through his servant David connects this chapter to the Bible's great story of salvation through a chosen king. The name Jesus comes from the same verb, to save. The chapter also shows the limits of David: he is anointed but weak, unable to restrain the violence of his own men, and he must leave vengeance to the LORD. Israel would later long for a son of David who would reign in perfect justice and be unstained by innocent blood (Isaiah 11:3-5). The New Testament proclaims Jesus as that king, whose own innocent blood, shed for others, speaks a better word than the blood that cried out for vengeance (Hebrews 12:24). The connection is a longing the chapter creates, not a prediction it makes.

hard.q: Why doesn't David punish Joab for murdering Abner?
hard.a: David curses Joab's house, forces him to mourn publicly, and declares the murder evil, but he does not remove or execute him. The text gives David's own explanation: though anointed, he is weak, and the sons of Zeruiah are too fierce for him. At this stage David's kingdom was fragile and depended on Joab's military skill and the loyalty of his family (Joab was David's nephew). Some readers see this as political realism; others see it as a failure of justice that the book deliberately records, since Joab will go on to kill again (Amasa in chapter 20) and to act against David's wishes (Absalom in chapter 18). On his deathbed David tells Solomon to deal with Joab (1 Kings 2:5-6), which shows that he never forgot the unpunished blood. The narrator neither excuses David nor condemns him outright, but lets the consequences speak.

questions: Joab's revenge was rooted in real grief for his brother. How can legitimate pain turn into something destructive when it is not handed over to God?
David mourned publicly for a man who had fought against him. What does honoring an opponent reveal about a person's character?
David confessed that he was weak even though he was anointed king. Where do you feel the gap between your calling and your ability to carry it out?
